I had a look at some diamonds given by @Jovan Gerbscheid's linter. And it looks like we have a problem with inferInstanceAs. It shows up in padics, for instance, but I guess it's not the only place:

#defeq_abuse in
example : ((instRingPadic p).toAddCommGroup) = instAddCommGroupPadic p := by
  with_reducible_and_instances rfl
/-
#defeq_abuse: command fails with `backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency true` but succeeds with `false`.
The following isDefEq checks are the root causes of the failure:
  ❌️ Ring.zsmul =?= instSubNegMonoidPadic._aux_9 p
-/

The issue is the following. Ring extends Semiring, AddCommGroup. The extension of AddCommGroup is flat, i.e., it only adds the fields that are not already in Semiring. In particular, Ring has a field zsmul : ℤ → G → G coming from SubNegMonoid. When doing deriving, this field is hidden behing a (non-reducible) function instRingPadic._aux_2, as it should. But this function is not related to the similar function instSubNegMonoidPadic._aux_9 p that shows up in the AddCommGroup instance. In fact they are the exact same function, but this is not noticeable at instance transparency.

mwe:

class Foo (α : Type) where
  a : α
  b : α

class Bar (α : Type) where
  b : α
  c : α

class FooBar (α : Type) extends Foo α, Bar α

instance : FooBar Nat where
  a := 0
  b := 1
  c := 2

def MyNat := Nat
deriving Foo, Bar, FooBar

/--
error: Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side
  instFooBarMyNat.toBar
is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side
  instBarMyNat

⊢ instFooBarMyNat.toBar = instBarMyNat
-/
#guard_msgs in
lemma zou : instFooBarMyNat.toBar = instBarMyNat := by
  with_reducible_and_instances rfl

@Kim Morrison , do you think that this is something that could/should be fixed at the deriving level? Or should we just create the instances by hand in these specific situations?
(An easy "fix" is to just do deriving Foo, FooBar and letting Bar be constructed automatically from the FooBar instance)
In your MWE b is declared twice independently, is this the case in the original example as well? I didn't even have it on my screen that we allow this...

Yes, absolutely. That's something that happens everywhere in the algebraic hierarchy, and for which the inheritance mechanism is explicitly designed. For instance, Ring extends Semiring and AddCommGroup which both have a zero, an addition, etc. The algorithm is that a Ring instance will have a function toSemiring to the semiring instance, and additional flat fields that correspond to the fields of AddCommGroup that are not in Semiring.

Maybe your question is about having this defined by a common class, instead of a common field? It's essentially the same, but maybe it corresponds more to your intuition:

class Base (α : Type) where
  b : α

class Foo (α : Type) extends Base α where
  a : α

class Bar (α : Type) extends Base α where
  c : α

class FooBar (α : Type) extends Foo α, Bar α

instance : FooBar Nat where
  a := 0
  b := 1
  c := 2

def MyNat := Nat
deriving Foo, Bar, FooBar

/--
error: Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side
  instFooBarMyNat.toBar
is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side
  instBarMyNat

⊢ instFooBarMyNat.toBar = instBarMyNat
-/
#guard_msgs in
lemma zou : instFooBarMyNat.toBar = instBarMyNat := by
  with_reducible_and_instances rfl

We typically have a common parent class that everything extends (e.g. Zero, Mul). But for zsmul and nsmul this wouldn't work, because we would be extending SMul twice. The solution would be to create a separate ZSMul and NSMul` type class, and then always extend this class.
Yes, I agree it would probably be a good idea to do this refactor anyway.

Yes exactly, thanks for the updated example
Ok I see now, indeed inferInstanceAs does not handle flat inheritance as nicely as structural... will have to think about this

I've been again bitten by this. But I've also encountered another weird behavior of deriving that I thought I would report here. It's a case where deriving shouldn't work, but instead it half-works without an error message, which is kind of hard to realize.

class Foo (α : Type)
class Bar (α : Type) [Foo α]

instance : Foo Nat where
instance : Bar Nat where

def MyNat : Type := Nat
deriving Bar -- no error message, seems to work, creates an instance

#synth Bar MyNat -- fails

Since the type copy MyNat has no instance of class Foo, deriving should complain that it can not create a Bar instance. But it has no problem to do that, happily using the Foo instance of Nat, and without any error message. Even more, if you do deriving Bar, Foo instead of the correct deriving Foo, Bar, then everything seems to work but in fact the instances are not correct and not usable. I agree it's a case of user error here, but since there are no warnings whatsoever it's still a little bit nasty of deriving. @Sebastian Ullrich
Indeed, I noticed this behaviour as well.

This is causing an unexpected unification failure in Mathlib.Topology.Algebra.Category.ProfiniteGrp.Basic, which now uses backward.inferInstanceAs.wrap false.

Another quirk about inferInstanceAs that I noticed when looking at the source code is that it doesn't check whether the new instance is defeq to the old one. That can give surprising behaviour, and in some cases kernel errors:

class A (α : Type) where
  a : α

class B (α : Type) extends A α where
  b : α
  a_eq_b : a = b

instance : B Nat where
  a := 3
  b := 3
  a_eq_b := rfl

def MyNat := Nat

instance : A MyNat where a := (5 : Nat)

instance : B MyNat := inferInstanceAs <| B Nat -- kernel error
Ah yes, #13346 was in preparation of this

Here is a #mwe. I can't say if this is expected behavior or not.

class Base (α : Type) where
  a : α

class Main0 (α : Type) extends Base α where
  b : α

class Main1 (α : Type) extends Base α where
  c : α

class Super (α : Type) extends Main0 α, Main1 α where

def MyCopy (α : Type) : Type := α

instance iBase (α : Type) [Base α] : Base (MyCopy α) :=
  inferInstanceAs <| Base α

instance iMain0 (α : Type) [Main0 α] : Main0 (MyCopy α) :=
  inferInstanceAs <| Main0 α

instance iMain1 (α : Type) [Main1 α] : Main1 (MyCopy α) :=
  inferInstanceAs <| Main1 α

instance iSuper (α : Type) [Super α] : Super (MyCopy α) :=
  inferInstanceAs <| Super α

example (α : Type) [Super α] :
    (iSuper α).toMain1 = iMain1 α := by
  with_reducible_and_instances rfl -- fails

We have 4 classes, with Base extended both by Main0 and Main1, and a superclass extending Main0 and Main1. Then we create a type copy MyCopy α, and for each of the 4 classes we record on MyCopy α the same instance as on α through inferInstanceAs. Then the diamond on the copy does not commute at implicit reducibility.

I claim that this is not the same issue as had been reported before. What the inferInstanceAs is doing here is just hiding the instance of α under a function, but this function is always implicit_reducible -- so, not really hiding anything. The diamond doesn't commute not because of the hiding function, because they're all transparent, but because the types don't match at some point between MyCopy α and α.

@Sebastian Ullrich , can you explain the rationale for the current behavior of not hiding anything in this kind of situation -- i.e., having a completely leaky instance? Would it make sense, also in this case, to see if the subclasses already have registered instances and to use them when available, and use non-reducible functions when it's not the case, to remove the leakiness?

To be clear, this is how it can be fixed:

class Base (α : Type) where
  a : α

class Main0 (α : Type) extends Base α where
  b : α

class Main1 (α : Type) extends Base α where
  c : α

class Super (α : Type) extends Main0 α, Main1 α where

def MyCopy (α : Type) : Type := α

instance iBase (α : Type) [Base α] : Base (MyCopy α) :=
  inferInstanceAs <| Base α

instance iMain0 (α : Type) [Main0 α] : Main0 (MyCopy α) :=
  inferInstanceAs <| Main0 α

instance iMain1 (α : Type) [i : Main1 α] : Main1 (MyCopy α) where
  c := i.c

instance iSuper (α : Type) [Super α] : Super (MyCopy α) where

example (α : Type) [Super α] :
    (iSuper α).toMain1 = iMain1 α := by
  with_reducible_and_instances rfl -- succeeds
I think allowing non-constructors (by eta-expanding them to a constructor) in fast_instance% would fix this?
(I think we discussed this before)

Yes, I know how to fix it by declaring instances by hand. But in this way the instances are still leaky (unless we also add opaque functions). I wonder if this is something we should work around in Mathlib (definitely possible, as you've just shown) or something that core would consider improving.

I think we should fix fast_instance so that the following is correct:

instance iMain0 (α : Type) [Main0 α] : Main0 (MyCopy α) :=
  fast_instance% ‹Main0 α›

instance iMain1 (α : Type) [Main1 α] : Main1 (MyCopy α) :=
  fast_instance% ‹Main1 α›

instance iSuper (α : Type) [Super α] : Super (MyCopy α) :=
  fast_instance% ‹Super α›

(of course it would be nice for core to handle this, but that has always been true of fast_instance%)
The awkward thing is that it may not always be desirable to eta expand in fast_instance%. In fact, I think the eta expansion is useful if and only if a subinstance can be synthesized and used.

The leakiness with the current implementation I'm mentioning is

example (α : Type) [h : Base α] :
    iBase α = h := by
  with_reducible_and_instances rfl -- works, while these are instances on different types!
And I think it wouldn't be fixed by fast_instance%, so we really need some inferInstanceAs opaque function here if we want to fix it.

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

In fact, I think the eta expansion is useful if and only if a subinstance can be synthesized and used.

Indeed, but this is a little easier to enforce by hand than whatever the current issue is
(at least in the initial implementation, fast_instance% was also only useful in that scenario anyway, as that was exactly its purpose)

Oh right, fast_instance% currently throws an error if the instance doesn't reduce to a constructor, so there are currently no uses where eta expansion would be bad.

We are in the slightly awkward situation that fast_instance% and inferInstanceAs have separate implementations of essentially the same algorithm, but both with different quirks. fast_instance% does not add unfolding boundaries in the way that inferInstanceAs does. We might be relying on this in some places, but in the long run it would be better to switch to, and improve, core's instance normalization function.

To me the fact that natural instances defined using inferInstanceAs lead to a diamond definitely counts as a bug, yes. But also I don't understand why inferInstanceAs hides the original instance behind a function, but this function is implicit reducible, so in fact it doesn't hide anything -- I would also count this as bug. But maybe it's a deliberate design on your side, I don't know.

Sebastian Ullrich said:

There is no simple way to check whether any subinstances already exist

Huh, I though this is exactly what inferInstanceAs was already doing? As in, reducing the expression to a constructor application, and trying to synthesize sub-instances. The only difference in this case is that you need to eta expance instead of reduce.
And you would do that speculatively or just keep the expansion in any case? Impact of that is unclear to me
I would keep the expansion if and only if a sub-instance was found.

I had a look at the mathlib branch of lean#13441. The category theory breakages can be fixed by putting backward.inferInstanceAs.wrap false in the instances for Category ((C ∘ f) j) and Category (Sum.elim C D s).

What goes wrong in the proofs is that a tactic like simp rewrites (C ∘ f) j to C (f j), or Sum.elim C D (.inl i) to C i. But the corresponding Category theory instance on these types is not changed. So now there are two different instances. But because of the new semireducible def in the instance, the data of the instances is not defeq in reducible_and_instances.
On the other hand, we could argue that actually Sum.elim and Function.comp should be implicit_reducible.
Either way, I think it won't be possible to pre-emptively fix everything that lean#13441 breaks. So another flood of new set_options in mathlib is the way to go I think.
